sourceLabel: Final Exam — practice (computer part), simple case
intro: The Final's graph programming section asks you to extend Graph<T> with a new traversal method on top of your Milestone 1 work. Practice that exact pattern by adding a public int numDirectedTriangles() method to your Graph<T> (or its AL/AM subclasses) that returns the number of directed 3-cycles in the graph — that is, ordered triples of distinct vertices (u, v, w) with edges u→v, v→w, w→u. Then paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java for a self-check. The simple 3-vertex case is the warm-up; harder variants follow.
hints: A directed triangle (u, v, w) requires three directed edges: u→v, v→w, and w→u. The simplest correct implementation iterates over all ordered triples of distinct vertices and checks the three edges via hasEdge — but it must not double-count.

The triple (A, B, C) and (B, C, A) and (C, A, B) describe the same triangle (a 3-cycle has three rotations). One way to count each triangle exactly once is to enforce a fixed ordering on the triple — e.g. require u to compare-less-than both v and w using vertex.toString().

If you're seeing 6 where the test expects 2, you're counting each triangle three times (once per rotation). Either divide by 3 at the end, or restrict to one canonical rotation per triangle as described above.

sourceLabel: Final Exam — practice (computer part), example graph
intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method as the warm-up, now on a 6-vertex example from the Final practice's computer part. The graph below has exactly 3 directed triangles after all 9 edges are added. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java after the simple case passes. If your count is wildly off, the bug is usually rotation-double-counting; if it's off by one or two, you may be misreading the edge list — sketch the adjacency list on paper first.
hints: Build the adjacency list on paper before running. From A: A→B. From B: B→C, B→D. From C: C→A, C→E, C→F. From D: D→E. From E: E→B, E→F. From F: nothing. With those edges in hand, scan for closed 3-cycles by inspection — that gives you the answer to compare against your code.

If you're seeing 9 instead of 3, you're counting each of the three triangles three times (one per rotation). If you're seeing 6 or 18, you're counting both rotations AND reflections — but in a directed graph there is no reflection symmetry, so check your loop bounds.

A reliable iteration shape: for u in keySet(), for v in successorSet(u), for w in successorSet(v) — if hasEdge(w, u) and {u,v,w} are pairwise distinct, increment. Then divide the running count by 3 once at the end.

sourceLabel: Final Exam — practice (computer part), large graph perf
intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.
